text:
Monsieur de Clèves could not withstand the state of prostration in which he found himself. A fever seized him that very night, with symptoms so severe that from that moment his illness appeared very dangerous. Madame de Clèves was informed of it; she came with all haste. When she arrived, he was even worse; she found him so cold and icy toward her that she was extremely surprised and distressed by it. It even seemed to her that he received the care she gave him with reluctance; but in the end, she thought that this was perhaps an effect of his illness.

As soon as she was in Blois, where the court then was, Monsieur de Nemours could not keep himself from feeling joy at knowing that she was in the same place as he. He tried to see her, and went every day to Monsieur de Clèves’s house, on the pretext of inquiring after his health; but it was in vain. She never left her husband’s room, and felt violent grief at the condition in which she saw him. Monsieur de Nemours was in despair that she was so distressed; he easily judged how greatly this distress renewed the affection she had for Monsieur de Clèves, and how greatly this affection created a dangerous diversion from the passion she had in her heart. This thought caused him mortal anguish for some time; but the extremity of Monsieur de Clèves’s illness opened new hopes to him. He saw that Madame de Clèves might perhaps be free to follow her inclination, and that he might find in the future a succession of lasting happiness and pleasures. He could not bear this thought, so much turmoil and transport did it cause him, and he turned his mind away from it for fear of finding himself too unhappy if he should lose his hopes.

Meanwhile, Monsieur de Clèves had been almost given up by the physicians. On one of the last days of his illness, after spending a very painful night, he said in the morning that he wished to rest. Madame de Clèves remained alone in his room; it seemed to her that instead of resting, he was very agitated. She approached and came to kneel before his bed, her face entirely covered with tears. Monsieur de Clèves had resolved not to show her the violent resentment he felt against her; but the care she gave him, and her distress, which sometimes appeared genuine to him and which he also sometimes regarded as signs of dissimulation and perfidy, caused such conflicting and painful feelings in him that he could not contain them within himself.

“You shed many tears, Madame,” he said to her, “for a death that you are causing, and which cannot give you the grief you make a show of feeling. I am no longer in a condition to reproach you,” he continued, in a voice weakened by illness and sorrow; “but I am dying of the cruel anguish you have caused me. Was an action as extraordinary as the one you performed in speaking to me at Coulommiers to have so little consequence? Why enlighten me about the passion you felt for Monsieur de Nemours, if your virtue did not extend far enough to resist it? I loved you to the point of being glad to be deceived, I confess it to my shame; I have regretted that false peace from which you roused me. Why did you not leave me in that tranquil blindness which so many husbands enjoy? I might have remained ignorant all my life that you loved Monsieur de Nemours. I shall die,” he added; “but know that you make death welcome to me, and that, after taking from me the esteem and tenderness I felt for you, life would fill me with horror. What would I do with life,” he went on, “if I were to spend it with a person whom I loved so much and by whom I have been so cruelly deceived, or if I were to live apart from that same person and come to an open rupture and to acts of violence so contrary to my disposition and to the passion I felt for you? It went beyond what you saw of it, Madame; I concealed the greater part of it from you, for fear of importuning you or of losing some part of your esteem through behavior unbecoming in a husband. In short, I deserved your heart; once again, I die without regret, since I was unable to possess it and can no longer desire it. Farewell, Madame; one day you will regret a man who loved you with a true and legitimate passion. You will feel the sorrow that reasonable people find in such attachments, and you will know the difference between being loved as I loved you and being loved by men who, in showing you love, seek only the honor of seducing you. But my death will leave you free,” he added, “and you will be able to make Monsieur de Nemours happy without its costing you any crimes. What does it matter,” he continued, “what will happen when I am no more, and must I be weak enough to turn my eyes toward it!”

Madame de Clèves was so far from imagining that her husband could harbor suspicions against her that she listened to all these words without understanding them, and with no other idea than that he was reproaching her for her inclination toward Monsieur de Nemours; at last, suddenly emerging from her blindness:

“I, guilty of crimes!” she cried. “Even the thought of them is unknown to me. The most austere virtue could inspire no conduct other than that which I have followed; and I have never performed any action of which I would not have wished you to be a witness.”

“Would you have wished,” Monsieur de Clèves replied, looking at her disdainfully, “that I had witnessed the nights you spent with Monsieur de Nemours? Ah! Madame, can it be you of whom I am speaking when I speak of a woman who has spent nights with a man?”

“No, Monsieur,” she replied; “no, it is not of me that you are speaking. I have never spent either nights or moments with Monsieur de Nemours. He has never seen me in private; I have never tolerated him or listened to him, and I would swear every oath to it...”

“Say no more,” Monsieur de Clèves interrupted; “false oaths or a confession would perhaps cause me equal pain.”
